sections.title: Page 3

summary.text: The foreword describes information, education and communication as a key part of AIDS prevention, especially for populations with high-risk behaviour in South-East Asia. It notes that heterosexual transmission predominates in the Region and that the course of the epidemic depends on well-planned IEC that motivates responsible sexual behaviour.

sections.extract: FOREWORD Information, Education and Communication (IEC) is one of the most essential components of an AIDS prevention programme. When planned well, within the context of an overall HIV/AIDS prevention and control programme, IEC can be a very effective intervention to bring about appropriate changes in behaviour, especially among populations with high-risk behaviour. In the South-East Asia Region of WHO, where the

summary.text: Introduces the guide by arguing that, with no cure for AIDS, prevention relies on understanding and changing sexual behaviour. It begins to define IEC as a broad range of approaches, activities and outputs beyond printed materials.

sections.extract: SEA/AIDS/81 1. INTRODUCTION The pandemic of Acquired Immuno-deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) poses a unique challenge to public health planners and programme developers. With no cure in sight, we are forced to look closely at behavioural patterns and how to alter them to prevent AIDS. Since AIDS is primarily a sexually transmitted disease (STD), it is important that policy-makers, communicators and public health

sections.title: Page 5

summary.text: Explains that IEC spans mass media, interpersonal communication, training and audience research, and describes how the guide is meant to help programme managers. It then outlines the projected growth of HIV infections in Asia, expected to exceed those in sub-Saharan Africa by 2000.

sections.extract: SEA/AIDS/81 Page 2 posters hanging on clinic walls, materials are only one component. Effective IEC makes use of a full range of approaches and activities. Approaches may range from the use of mass media to inform or establish positive norms among the general population to the use of targeted interpersonal communication to help those at particular risk evaluate their own behaviour and develop new personal skills.

sections.title: Page 7

summary.text: Introduces a behavioural change model with stages from unaware to adopting new behaviour, illustrated with safer sex, and notes how awareness can be raised among different groups.

sections.extract: SEA/AIDS/81 Page 4 3.1 Process of Behavioural Change : A Continuum Bringing about a behavioural change is, however, a difficult process. The task is further complicated by the sensitive and personal nature of the issues, dealing as they largely do with sex and sexuality. A variety of approaches and messages will be needed to promote movement of individuals and populations along the continuum of behavioural change.

sections.title: Page 8

summary.text: Describes the middle stages of the behaviour change continuum: becoming concerned, gaining knowledge and skills, and trying new behaviour. It stresses that targeted and interpersonal approaches work better than mass media for creating concern, and that condom negotiation and use skills are essential.

sections.extract: SEA/AIDS/81 Page 5 Concerned It is possible to be aware without being concerned. Information must be given is such a way that the audience feels it applies to them, i.e., the audience becomes concerned, and people are motivated to evaluate their own behaviour. summary.text: Covers the final stage of adopting and sustaining new behaviour, then sets out roles of IEC in STD and AIDS prevention. These include informing and motivating at-risk groups, reaching intermediaries and reducing stigma and discrimination against people with HIV.

sections.extract: SEA/AIDS/81 Page 6 Adoption of New Behaviour Finally, the individual decides to remain faithful to one faithful partner or regularly uses condoms as a source of protection from AIDS/STD. Assuming the new behaviour continues to be evaluated as largely positive, sustained behavioural change could take place at this stage. Continuous messages of support and access to condoms are still essential. Programmes must ensure

summary.text: Notes IEC support for STD services, voluntary blood donation and universal precautions, then begins a section on lessons from IEC experience. It warns that campaigns blaming particular groups such as sex workers and drug users can be counterproductive.

sections.extract: SEA/AIDS/81 Page 7 (3) Support for various components of an AIDS Prevention and Control Programme: IEC campaigns can promote seeking of quality STD services, which of course must be made available. IEC can also support efforts to promote voluntary blood donation and the implementation of universal precautions in health care settings. 4. summary.text: Describes evaluation and reprogramming after each campaign cycle and notes that a mass campaign is only one part of an IEC programme.

sections.extract: SEA/AIDS/81 Page 35 Evaluation and Reprogramming: After the completion of the campaign cycle, a repeat baseline evaluation should be conducted along with a study to produce some qualitative data on the impact of the campaign. The data should be analysed and fed into reprogramming of the next cycle of the awareness campaign. Messages will change from straight information to more specific behavioural change messages
